The supplied material consists entirely of front matter for C. W. C. Oman’s historical volume on the Byzantine Empire. The initial pages contain library stamps and ownership marks from the University of California [PDF p. 2]. The title page identifies the work as *The Byzantine Empire* within the series *The Story of the Nations* [PDF p. 11]. C. W. C. Oman is credited as the author, holding degrees and fellowships at Oxford University [PDF p. 11]. His previous works include studies on medieval warfare and historical biography [PDF p. 11]. The publication details list G. P. Putnam’s Sons in New York and T. Fisher Unwin in London [PDF p. 11]. Copyright records confirm the year of publication as 1892 for both American and British editions [PDF p. 12].

Oman’s preface addresses the shifting historiographical reputation of Byzantium [PDF p. 13]. He notes that fifty years prior, the term "Byzantine" implied corruption and decadence to modern historians [PDF p. 13]. Edward Gibbon had previously dismissed the empire as a series of vicious weaklings following Justinian [PDF p. 13]. Oman argues that this negative view persisted for generations without significant challenge [PDF p. 13]. He credits George Finlay’s monumental work from 1856 with beginning to correct these misconceptions [PDF p. 13]. J. B. Bury’s volumes, published in 1889, further aided this revisionist perspective for English readers [PDF p. 13].

The author states his intention to follow the spirit of Finlay and Bury rather than Gibbon [PDF p. 13]. He acknowledges a heavy debt to these two scholars for making his task feasible [PDF p. 14]. Oman admits he did not consult every chronicler of the Eastern realm personally [PDF p. 14]. However, he claims sufficient acquaintance with key sources like Procopius and Anna Comnena [PDF p. 14]. The preface is dated February 1892 from Oxford [PDF p. 14].

The table of contents outlines twenty-six chapters covering the empire’s entire lifespan [PDF p. 15]. It begins with the foundation of Byzantium and its destruction in A.D. 196 [PDF p. 15]. The structure moves through Constantine’s founding of Constantinople between A.D. 328 and 330 [PDF p. 15]. Subsequent entries detail conflicts with Goths, Huns, Slavs, and Saracens [PDF p. 16]. The list includes social history sections on religion and monasticism from A.D. 320 to 620 [PDF p. 17]. Later chapters address the Iconoclast controversy and the Macedonian dynasty’s literary emperors [PDF p. 18].

The contents conclude with the Latin conquest of Constantinople in 1204 [PDF p. 19]. It traces the decline under the restored empire and the rise of Ottoman Turks [PDF p. 19]. The final chapter covers the fall of Constantinople in A.D. 1453 [PDF p. 20]. An index follows the main text on page 351 according to this list [PDF p. 20].

A detailed list of illustrations accompanies the contents [PDF p. 21]. Many images are sourced from Charles Bayet’s *L’Art Byzantin* published in Paris in 1883 [PDF p. 21]. The frontispiece depicts the interior of St. Sophia [PDF p. 7]. Other plates show coins, statues, and architectural details of Constantinople [PDF p. 21]. Some illustrations feature specific emperors like Justinian II or Romanus Diogenes [PDF p. 23]. The list ends with a plate titled *Angel of the Night* on page 350 [PDF p. 24].

This summary relies exclusively on front matter, prefaces, and lists provided in the source. No narrative chapters are included in the supplied text. Readers cannot assess Oman’s actual treatment of Byzantine history from these pages alone.

The narrative begins with the legendary founding of Byzantium by Dorian Greeks from Megara [PDF p. 27]. These settlers sought wealth in the Black Sea region, guided by myths of the Golden Fleece and Amazons [PDF p. 28]. They established a colony on a headland near the Golden Horn, following an oracle’s advice to build opposite the "city of the blind" [PDF p. 29]. This referred to Chalcedonians who had previously chosen a less strategic site across the strait [PDF p. 29]. The author argues that Byzantium’s location was militarily and commercially superior, commanding trade routes between Europe and Asia [PDF p. 30]. Its natural defenses made it nearly impregnable, falling only to famine or treachery in early history [PDF p. 30].

Byzantium maintained independence for three centuries, except during Persian occupation [PDF p. 31]. It played a role in the Ionic Revolt and was later liberated by Greek forces after Salamis [PDF p. 31]. The city briefly allied with Athens but suffered sieges during the Peloponnesian War [PDF p. 32]. Internal history remains obscure, though unique customs like iron currency are noted [PDF p. 32]. Ancient chroniclers depicted Byzantines as luxurious and gluttonous, a characterization the author dismisses as neighborly envy [PDF p. 33]. The city resisted Philip of Macedon, adopting the crescent and star emblem after a miraculous light saved them from siege [PDF p. 33].

After Alexander’s death, Byzantium passed through various hands before allying with Rome [PDF p. 34]. It retained freedom as a confederate city until Emperor Vespasian revoked its privileges in A.D. 71 [PDF p. 34]. The city flourished under the Pax Romana but faced destruction during civil wars following Commodus’s murder [PDF p. 35]. Severus besieged and sacked Byzantium in A.D. 196, executing leaders and demolishing walls [PDF p. 35]. Caracalla later restored self-governance, yet Gothic incursions continued to plague the region [PDF p. 36].

The city recovered under Illyrian emperors but became a battleground between Licinius and Maximinus Daza [PDF p. 37]. Licinius fortified Byzantium as his chief stronghold against Constantine [PDF p. 37]. Constantine besieged the city in A.D. 323, using military engines to force surrender [PDF p. 38]. This victory united the Roman Empire under one ruler for the first time since Diocletian’s partitions [PDF p. 39]. The author portrays Constantine as a pragmatic administrator who lacked reverence for Rome’s ancient prestige [PDF p. 40]. He viewed Italy as secondary to his Danubian and Gallic holdings, seeking a new administrative center [PDF p. 41].

Rome was strategically inconvenient due to distance from Balkan frontiers and poor harbors [PDF p. 42]. Constantine needed a site accessible by land and sea that could serve as an impregnable arsenal [PDF p. 42]. He considered Naissus and Sardica but rejected them for being too close to the frontier or lacking sea access [PDF p. 42]. The text ends abruptly while listing these potential sites, leaving the final selection process incomplete in this excerpt.

The source material concludes mid-sentence during Constantine’s site evaluation, offering no further details on his decision-making process beyond initial rejections. Consequently, the specific criteria leading to the ultimate choice of Byzantium remain unexplained within the provided pages.

Constantine evaluated several potential sites for his new imperial capital before selecting Byzantium [PDF p. 43]. Nicomedia offered an eligible location and had previously served as an imperial residence [PDF p. 43]. However, Constantine wished to avoid eclipsing the memory of Diocletian in that city [PDF p. 43]. Christians associated Nicomedia with the persecutions under Diocletian and Galerius [PDF p. 43]. Ilium possessed only legendary glories and lacked a suitable harbor for naval command [PDF p. 43]. Byzantium was thoroughly familiar to Constantine from his military campaigns in the region [PDF p. 43]. The emperor recognized its significant military advantages during his months stationed nearby [PDF p. 43]. Despite this logic, the Roman world reacted with surprise to the choice of a provincial fortress [PDF p. 43].

Once decided, Constantine marked the city limits through solemn processions in traditional Roman style [PDF p. 44]. A later legend describes him tracing fortifications with his spear while walking westward [PDF p. 44]. His attendants questioned the vast scale of the plan as he moved further from old gates [PDF p. 44]. Constantine claimed an invisible guide directed his steps until the boundary was complete [PDF p. 44]. He included all seven hills on the peninsula between the Propontis and Golden Horn [PDF p. 44]. The site of his former siege tent became the marketplace for the new foundation [PDF p. 44]. There he erected the Milion, a golden milestone measuring distances across the eastern world [PDF p. 45]. This structure housed statues of Constantine and his mother Helena within a temple-like building [PDF p. 45].

The imperial palace occupied the south-eastern part of old Byzantium on cleared land [PDF p. 45]. A wall separated this vast precinct from the rest of the city near the Lighthouse [PDF p. 45]. The Augustaeum served as a central forum paved with marble and surrounded by buildings [PDF p. 45]. Three structures connected by colonnades stood between the palace and this open space [PDF p. 45]. The Baths of Zeuxippus were enlarged using ancient statues from Greece and Asia [PDF p. 47]. These included masterpieces like the Athene of Lyndus and the Zeus of Dodona [PDF p. 47]. Constantine also established a Senate House modeled on that of Old Rome [PDF p. 47]. He attracted senatorial families eastward through gifts of pensions and houses [PDF p. 47]. The Patriarch’s Palace lay nearby but remained overshadowed by the imperial residence [PDF p. 48]. This proximity prevented the bishop from gaining independent spiritual authority like his Roman counterpart [PDF p. 48].

The Hippodrome dominated the western side of the Augustaeum with its massive dimensions [PDF p. 48]. Chariot races between the Blues and Greens factions became a central feature of civic life [PDF p. 48]. This rivalry extended beyond sports into religious and political conflicts throughout history [PDF p. 48]. The emperor’s box, or Kathisma, allowed frequent public appearances from his throne [PDF p. 50]. Notable events included the crowning of rebel Hypatius by an impromptu mob [PDF p. 50]. Justinian II later sat there with defeated rivals bound beneath his footstool [PDF p. 50]. The central spina displayed monuments including an Egyptian obelisk and a brazen serpent [PDF p. 50].

The text presents a narrative that blends historical fact with later legendary accounts of the city’s founding [PDF p. 44]. Specific details about the Senate House are missing because it was destroyed twice within a century [PDF p. 47]. The author interprets the physical layout as evidence of Constantine’s desire to control religious authority [PDF p. 48].
